analysis.one_liner: Repeals the hydraulic-fracturing exemption from drinking-water rules and requires fracking companies to disclose their chemicals.
analysis.headline: After a subcommittee hearing in April 2011, the bill with 11 cosponsors never received a Senate committee vote and expired when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking wells, whose drinking water and health could be affected. Requiring companies to list every chemical used, post the lists publicly, and hand over secret formulas to doctors in a medical emergency would let residents and physicians find out what is being injected underground near their homes.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Safe Drinking Water Act exemption so that fluids injected during hydraulic fracturing count as "underground injection," which brings the practice under federal drinking-water protections [S2][S3].

Requires companies to disclose, before drilling begins and again after operations end, a full list of chemicals to be used or used — including chemical identification numbers, safety data sheets, and volumes [S3].
Requires states or the EPA to make those chemical disclosures available to the public, including posting them online [S3].

Requires companies to immediately hand over proprietary or trade-secret chemical formulas to a treating physician or nurse during a medical emergency, regardless of any confidentiality agreement, so doctors can treat exposure victims [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would bear new compliance costs and would operate under federal drinking-water rules for the first time, which industry argued could slow drilling and raise production costs. The bill does protect one thing companies care about: it does not require public disclosure of proprietary chemical formulas, and it lets companies demand confidentiality paperwork after an emergency disclosure [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and drillers

drawbacks.text: Treating fracking as "underground injection" under the Safe Drinking Water Act would add federal permitting and oversight to wells previously handled outside that law, a change industry warned could raise costs and slow natural gas production [S2][S3].

Companies would keep proprietary formulas out of public view — the bill explicitly bars states or the EPA from forcing public disclosure of a trade-secret formula, so neighbors still would not see everything going into the ground except in an emergency [S3].

States that already run their own fracking chemical-disclosure programs would face an added federal baseline, which critics saw as duplicative regulation of an activity states were beginning to police themselves [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is direct: residents near wells and doctors treating exposure would learn which chemicals were used, and fracking would lose its unusual exemption from a law that covers comparable underground injections. The costs fall on producers in added compliance and oversight, though the bill is deliberately gentle on trade secrets — it protects proprietary formulas from public disclosure even while forcing emergency disclosure to doctors. The strongest honest objection is that added federal permitting could slow drilling, which some states and producers argued was unnecessary as states built their own disclosure rules.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which held a subcommittee hearing in April 2011 but never voted to advance it, and it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Casey introduced the FRAC Act in the Senate on March 15, 2011 [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the day it was introduced [S5].
On April 12, 2011, the committee's Subcommittee on Water and Wildlife held a hearing on the bill (S.Hrg. 112-901) [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill was never reported out of committee, never reached the Senate floor, and expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers, who kept the hydraulic-fracturing exemption from federal drinking-water law and kept their chemical mixes out of public view. People living near fracking wells got no federal right to know what was injected underground.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers using hydraulic fracturing
industries.note: The bill would end the industry's exemption from the Safe Drinking Water Act and force it to disclose every chemical injected underground. Companies fought to keep the exemption and their chemical secrecy, a position that runs directly against residents' ability to know what is being pumped near their water supplies.

Suppliers whose chemical blends were shielded as trade secrets would have to register ingredients with the state or EPA and reveal formulas to doctors in emergencies. The bill preserves trade secrets from the public, so the loss is limited to regulator and physician access.
